name: private-class-data
intent: Keep an object's data readable but not writable after construction by moving it into a separate holder object that exposes read access only, so that neither the object's own methods nor its subclasses can assign the fields.
problem: Fields that must not change after construction are still writable: they cannot be declared read-only because their values are computed or validated while the constructor runs, or they are protected or package-visible so every method of the class and of its subclasses can assign them - and one stray assignment then silently breaks the invariant the constructor established.
context: Objects whose invariant is fixed at construction time but whose state must stay readable: value-like domain objects, credential, session and configuration holders, geometry or parameter objects consulted by many methods, and base classes of a hierarchy whose state subclasses should only read. It applies where no single declaration withdraws write access, or where the write privilege has to be removed from methods that legitimately read the data.
benefits: Write access after construction is withdrawn structurally: only the holder's constructor can assign, so an accidental assignment in any method of the owner class - or in a subclass that cannot even name the holder's fields - fails to compile or fails immediately.
Gives 'final after construction' semantics to fields that cannot be declared read-only because their values are computed or validated while the constructor runs.
Reading stays as convenient as writing was: the holder exposes getters, so the owner's methods and clients keep reading the state without seeing how it is stored.
Shrinks the exposure surface: clients depend on the owner's accessors and behaviour instead of on individual attributes, so the representation can change without breaking callers.
Concentrates initialization and validation in one constructor, where the invariant is established once instead of being re-established by every writer.
Decouples the methods that share the attributes: they now depend on one holder's read interface instead of on each other's writes.
tradeoffs: One indirection and one extra object per instance - plus an allocation wherever the holder is allocated separately - and one accessor call per read; only inlining, JIT or LTO removes that cost.

It separates data from the behaviour that uses it, producing an anemic holder: invariants spanning state and logic are no longer owned by the state, and the design drifts back toward a struct plus service.

It fights frameworks that populate or mutate objects behind the API: JavaBeans, ORMs, serializers and mapping layers usually need a no-argument constructor, a setter or a proxy, and silently fall back to reflection when they find none.

Read-only-ness is shallow in most languages: a leaked reference to a mutable list, map or array re-opens the write path, so every mutable component needs a defensive copy or an unmodifiable view, at a cost per construction.

Every field needs an accessor on the holder and a forwarding accessor on the owner, and equality, hashing, cloning, comparison and debug rendering must be maintained across two objects instead of one.
Subclasses lose access to the state altogether in the strong realizations, so extension has to be redesigned around the owner's API (hooks, template methods) rather than around protected fields.

participants.responsibility: Owns one holder instance, creates and initializes it in its constructor, implements the public behaviour and forwards every read of the state to the holder; it keeps no writable copy of the data.
Holds the attributes, exposes them through getters (a setter only for attributes that must legitimately keep changing) and confines write privilege to its own initialization.
Reads through the target's behaviour and accessors and never receives a writable reference to the holder or to its mutable contents.
Extends the target without being able to write the state; in the strong realizations it cannot even name the holder's fields, so new behaviour must go through the target's API.

use_cases: Credential and session objects whose secret fields are read by many methods but must not be reassigned after login.
Value-like domain objects (money, measurements, a report's fixed filter parameters) whose components are validated and normalized in the constructor and never change afterwards.
Objects that are cached, compared for equality or serialized, where an accidental write would silently corrupt a cache entry or an equality contract.
Base classes of a template-method hierarchy in which the base declares the state once and the subclasses' overrides may only read it.
Graphical and geometry objects (the canonical circle example) whose size, colour and origin are used by drawing and measuring methods that must not modify them.
Snapshots and undo records handed to other components as a read-only view of a larger mutable model.

The Java Design Patterns project's ImmutableStew and StewData example: constructor-owned record state is read by behaviour but cannot be mutated by the target, making the strict holder form suitable for value-like snapshots and validated constructor inputs.

Qt Core's QSharedDataPointer and EmployeeData idiom: a public value class delegates storage to private data with const reads and copy-on-write writes, making this holder variant useful when sharing and independent mutation matter more than strict freezing.

libcamera::Extensible public classes and nested Private classes: a d-pointer keeps private state opaque to API users while allowing ABI-stable extension, making the access-controlled holder form suitable when a public hierarchy must evolve without exposing layout.
avoid_when: The language already offers the read-only declaration for exactly this purpose - const, final, val, let, readonly, get-only or init-only properties, records: a holder class on top of them is pure overhead.

The state legitimately changes after construction (an entity's lifecycle): use validated setters, or an explicit operation that returns a new value (immutable-object, copy-on-write) instead of freezing the field in place.

A persistence, mapping or UI framework must populate the object through reflection or property setters: give the framework a DTO or the mapping hooks it needs rather than fighting it with a frozen holder.
Only one or two simple attributes are involved and neither subclasses nor external readers exist: ordinary private fields with the usual accessors already cover the requirement.
anti_patterns: A data holder whose every attribute has a setter: the write privilege the pattern was meant to withdraw is handed back and one class has become two.
Getters that return the holder's mutable collections or arrays, re-opening the write path through the escaped reference.
A god holder: moving unrelated fields into one private Data object 'because state should be hidden', producing a nested class with no cohesion of its own.
Freezing state that has to evolve and then adding re-initialization or reset methods, so the object claims immutability while staying mutable.
Using the pattern to hide secrets from hostile code: reflection, unsafe blocks, instance_variable_set and serialization all bypass it, so secrets need key management, not a holder.
design_principles: Information hiding and encapsulation: expose the narrowest readable interface instead of the representation.
Separation of concerns: representation lives in the holder, behaviour in the target, so either can change without the other.
Fail fast and design by contract: an illegal write becomes a compile-time or immediate runtime failure instead of silent corruption.
Least privilege: write access is granted only during initialization, where the value is actually established.
Composition over inheritance for sharing state: subclasses read through the target's API instead of reaching into protected fields.
best_practices: Try the language's read-only declaration first (const, final, val, let, readonly, init-only properties, records, private fields with accessors); introduce a separate holder only when the value must be computed or validated before it becomes read-only, or when write access has to be withdrawn from a whole hierarchy.

Copy every mutable argument in the holder's constructor (a defensive copy, or an immutable copy such as List.copyOf, ImmutableArray or a frozen value type) and hand out copies or unmodifiable views - never the holder's own containers.
Make the holder private (nested, module-private, package-private or name-mangled) and name it after the state it protects (CircleData, SessionState) instead of a generic Data.
Expose behaviour rather than a getter per field wherever possible, so the representation stays hidden and callers cannot become dependent on the holder's shape.
Replace the holder instead of mutating it when the state must change (copy-on-write, or return a new target), so the read-only guarantee never needs an exception.
Write down which invariant the holder protects and why it is frozen; otherwise the next maintainer reintroduces a setter.
